verdict.reasoning: The changed AGENTS.md line names the literal checkout-relative path `.git/metareview/runs/` while asserting it is in Git's common directory and shared across worktrees. In a linked worktree, `.git` is a file pointing to the worktree-specific Git directory, so appending `/metareview/runs/` does not resolve. The common location must be obtained via Git, such as `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, or documented relative to the main worktree's Git directory. Thus the new documentation gives linked-worktree readers a nonexistent path.

The finding is grounded in the diff. Before this change, RowFor wrote FSMRunDir as `.metareview/runs/<id>/`, documented as relative to the old store root. New rows use `metareview/runs/<id>/` relative to the git common directory, but MigrateLegacyRows passes each decoded legacy Row unchanged to appendRow. Therefore migrated rows retain the old relative path, which resolves under the common directory to `<common>/.metareview/runs/<id>/` instead of the new `<common>/metareview/runs/<id>/`. The migration must normalize FSMRunDir or consumers will receive inconsistent and incorrect paths.

The test creates .metareview/runs/.torn under a plain t.TempDir(), not a Git repository. LegacyRunsPending can therefore return false because repo.StoreDir fails, regardless of whether .torn bookkeeping is correctly ignored. The displayed tests do not otherwise exercise that bookkeeping case in a valid repository, so this assertion is satisfied by the wrong condition and does not pin the stated property.

The diff explicitly allows init work_dir to be any directory inside a worktree, but mine() determines ownership only by calling repo.Toplevel(r.workDir). If that recorded subdirectory no longer exists, the lookup fails and the code treats the run as unattributable, so it is included only when here == main. Thus an existing linked worktree can stop reporting its own abandoned run merely because the original subdirectory was deleted, violating the stated worktree-scoping behavior.

The scan order creates a concrete TOCTOU gap: it reads the new shared store first and the legacy store second. If a concurrent FSM command moves a legacy run into the shared store after the first read but before the second, neither read observes that run, so discovery can falsely report no blocker. This function takes no lock and performs no rescan or snapshot validation to prevent that omission.

findings.issue: mine() runs repo.Toplevel on the nearest existing ancestor of a run's work_dir without checking that the toplevel belongs to this repository (same git common dir); for a removed linked worktree whose parent lies inside an unrelated git repo, Toplevel returns that repo and the here==main fallback is never reached.
findings.consequence: The abandoned run is attributed to a foreign toplevel matching no worktree of this repo and disappears from every checkout's status and Stop gate.

verdict.reasoning: The finding follows directly from the new logic. When work_dir no longer exists, existingAncestor may climb into a parent directory belonging to an unrelated Git repository. repo.Toplevel then succeeds for that foreign repository, so mine() does not use its error fallback and returns false unless that foreign toplevel coincidentally equals here. Consequently, the shared-store run is excluded from the main checkout and every linked worktree, violating the stated invariant that unattributable runs are reported from the main checkout.

findings.issue: Each abandoned run costs two uncached git subprocesses (StoreDir then Toplevel), not memoized per ancestor dir although many runs share a work_dir.
findings.consequence: Status and Stop-hook latency grows as about 2 x abandoned runs across all worktrees (the store is shared); seconds once stale runs reach the low hundreds.
